one_liner: One-function AES-NI 128-bit hash for x86-64; 1.4-2.5x XXH3 bulk throughput, but 3-4x slower on small keys.
what_it_does: falkhash is a non-cryptographic 128-bit hash the author wrote for his falkervisor code-coverage database: an experiment, not a maintained library. The whole API is one C function, __m128i falkhash(void *buf, uint64_t len, uint64_t seed), which returns the hash as an SSE vector. It has no header, and falkhash.c also contains a benchmark main(). It is not a drop-in for xxh3 or wyhash: the signature differs, the output is a 128-bit vector, and there is no streaming API.
how_it_is_fast: It consumes 80-byte chunks. Five unaligned 16-byte loads are XORed with the 128-bit seed and squeezed into one lane by a chain of AESENC rounds that uses the other four blocks as round keys, plus one more round keyed with the seed. The result is folded into the running hash with a single AESENC. Each AESENC is a full AES round (SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, key XOR) in one instruction, and per-chunk chains do not depend on the running hash, so from the source only one AESENC per 80 bytes sits on the loop-carried path. Four more seed-keyed AESENC rounds finalize, and the 0x50 chunk size was tuned for AMD family 15h, per the asm comment.
when_to_use: Bulk hashing of large buffers (tens of KB and up: coverage bitmaps, file chunks, snapshots) on x86-64 with AES-NI, where bytes per cycle matter more than per-call latency.
Non-adversarial content fingerprinting that wants a native 128-bit result at bulk speed: SMHasher3 measures 18.43 bytes/cycle for v2 vs 12.82 for XXH3-64 and 12.43 for MeowHash.
Internal tools or experiments where copying one small public-domain function is easier than adding a dependency, and portability beyond x86 does not matter.
when_not_to_use: Short keys or hash-table lookups: every input under 80 bytes is zero-padded to a full 80-byte block, giving 85.87 cycles/hash on 1-32 B keys in SMHasher3 (XXH3-64: 30.69) and 122.70 vs 29.46 for xxh3 in rurban SMHasher. Issue #2, asking about 64-bit integer keys, is unanswered.

Anything adversarial or security-related: the README says it is not crypto and was made 'by randomly testing things until it passed all of smhasher's tests', and funny-falcon's PR #1 pointed out a route to seed-independent collisions in v1, and the suggested fix (XOR every block with the seed) went into v2.

When you need a clean quality record: v2 fails 6 of 250 SMHasher3 tests (Sparse), and rurban rates the v1 asm POOR, with full 64-bit collisions on sparse 160-bit and 512-bit keys. MeowHash passes all 250 SMHasher3 tests at 12.43 bytes/cycle.
Non-x86 targets or CPUs without AES-NI: there is no fallback path; it includes x86 intrinsics headers and needs -maes.
When you need a maintained, packaged library: no commits since November 2015, no header or build target, no tests beyond a benchmark main().

integration.form: source-drop (copy the falkhash() function out of falkhash.c)
integration.dependencies: none (C standard library plus compiler x86 intrinsics headers)
integration.min_toolchain: Any C compiler with AES-NI intrinsics; the README reports GCC 4.9.2, clang 3.5.0, MSVC 18.00 and 19.00 (VS2013/VS2015); GCC/Clang need -maes
integration.platforms: x86 / x86-64 with AES-NI (designed for AMD64); no ARM or portable fallback
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. falkhash() is a pure function with only stack state, so concurrent calls look safe (inferred from source).

gotchas: Hash values changed between v1 (hand-written asm) and v2 (C intrinsics). rurban's 52401.48 MiB/s figure is for the v1 asm object; SMHasher3 benchmarks both versions (v2: 18.43 bytes/cycle; v1: 19.88).
The result is an __m128i, not an integer: store it with _mm_storeu_si128, and take the low 64-bit lane if you need a size_t hash, as rurban's wrapper does. The buffer parameter is a non-const void*.
falkhash.c defines main(), so compiling the file as-is into a program or library clashes with your own main(); extract the function.

Length is folded into the seed (high lane = seed + len + 1), which is what keeps zero-padded tails of different lengths apart. The only key is a 64-bit seed XORed into every block, so there is no DoS-resistance claim.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among the catalogued AES-NI hashes, falkhash v2 is roughly tied with gxhash in bulk (SMHasher3 18.43 vs 19.56 bytes/cycle) but fails fewer tests (6 vs 25), and it is about 1.5x MeowHash's bulk speed. Pick it over them only for a tiny vendored C function on x86-64 with large inputs; pick MeowHash for a clean SMHasher3 record, and XXH3, wyhash or rapidhash for small keys or portability.
verified_claims_summary: rurban SMHasher (AMD Ryzen 5 3350G, 262144-byte keys, compiler not stated, prebuilt nasm object of the v1 asm) gives falkhash 52401.48 MiB/s vs xxh3 20853.74 (~2.5x), wyhash 22640.53 (~2.3x) and City128 14472.20 (~3.6x), but 122.70 vs 29.46 cycles/hash on small keys. SMHasher3 (hardware not stated) on the current v2 C code gives 18.43 bytes/cycle vs XXH3-64 12.82 (~1.4x), wyhash 6.98 (~2.6x) and CityHash-64 4.75 (~3.9x).
status_note: Abandoned since November 2015 (48 stars, one unanswered 2023 issue), but Unlicense/public domain (no patent grant) and a hash function of about 80 lines that is trivial to vendor; the last compilers the author reports are GCC 4.9.2, clang 3.5.0 and MSVC 2015.
